echoes.note: The deliberate procurement and riding of a young donkey into Jerusalem evokes Zechariah's humble king who comes 'lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt the foal of a donkey.' Mark does not quote it (unlike Matthew/John), but the staged colt-riding has high coherence with the messianic peace-king imagery, and the theme recurs across the entry tradition. Volume is strong despite the missing citation.

Jacob's blessing of Judah, 'binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' supplies an old messianic-royal association of the bound colt that Second-Temple readers connected to the coming ruler of Judah (Gen 49:10). Mark's emphatically tied, never-ridden colt that is untied coheres with this figural Judahic kingship, though the link is mediated and contested.

The crowd's cry 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' formally cites the Hallel pilgrimage acclamation, where 'Hosanna' (hoshia-na, 'save now') is Ps 118:25 and the blessing is 118:26. This is a verbatim liturgical quotation with maximal volume; the same psalm recurs as the rejected-stone text in Mark 12:10-11, strengthening recurrence.

Spreading garments on the road as Jesus rides echoes the acclamation of Jehu, where the people 'took every man his garment, and put it under him... and blew the trumpet, saying, Jehu is king.' The shared royal-enthronement gesture of garments under the new king gives coherence to reading the entry as a kingmaking, though Mark adds the cut branches.

The crowd hails 'the coming kingdom of our father David,' invoking the Davidic covenant promise of an enduring throne and kingdom for David's offspring. The Davidic-dynastic frame of the entry coheres with Nathan's oracle, the foundational text for messianic kingship, though Mark cites no words from it.

The king's approach to Jerusalem and entry into the temple faintly recalls the processional liturgy of the King of glory entering the gates. The coherence is thematic (royal advent into the sanctuary), but there is no verbal contact, so the echo is faint and contested.

Mark situates the entry at the Mount of Olives, the very site where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of his eschatological coming. The geographic note may be loaded with this Day-of-the-LORD coherence, but the topographic detail is also simply realistic, so the allusion is contested.

Jesus' cursing of the fruitless fig tree enacts Jeremiah's judgment oracle, 'there shall be no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade,' where Israel's barrenness brings consuming judgment. The fig-tree-as-Israel symbolism has high coherence and recurs throughout the prophets, framing the act as a prophetic sign against the temple it brackets.

The prophet's lament 'there is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the firstripe fig' supplies the disappointed seeking of early fruit and finding none, a precise match for Jesus hungering and finding only leaves. The coherence is strong with Micah's portrait of a fruitless, faithless people awaiting judgment.

Hosea recalls finding Israel 'like the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time,' a metaphor of early promise turned to apostasy and barrenness (Hos 9:16, 'their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit'). The dried-up-root motif coheres tightly with the tree withered from the roots in 11:20, reinforcing the figural reading.

Joel's judgment imagery includes the LORD laying waste the vine and barking the fig tree so that its branches are made white, part of a Day-of-the-LORD agricultural desolation. The shared fig-tree-judgment field adds recurrence, though the verbal contact is faint and the theme is widely diffused, so the link is contested.

Jeremiah's vision of good and bad figs sorts Judah for blessing or judgment, supplying a prophetic precedent for figs symbolizing the nation's fate before the LORD. The coherence with Mark's fig sign-act against the temple is thematic rather than verbal, hence faint and contested.

Jesus' teaching 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations' is a verbatim citation of Isaiah's oracle gathering foreigners and outcasts to worship at the temple. Mark uniquely preserves 'for all the nations,' heightening the inclusion theme; the formal quotation has maximal volume and frames the cleansing as eschatological restoration.

The charge 'you have made it a den of robbers' formally quotes Jeremiah's temple sermon, where the people treat the LORD's house as a robbers' hideout while presuming on its protection. The citation imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction (Jer 7:14), giving the act prophetic-judgment force; high volume and tight coherence.

Zechariah closes with the promise that on the day of the LORD 'there shall be no more the Canaanite (trader/merchant) in the house of the LORD of hosts.' Jesus' expulsion of the buyers, sellers, and money-changers enacts this eschatological purging of commerce from the temple, a strong coherence often noted as the act's interpretive key.

Malachi's Lord who 'shall suddenly come to his temple' to purify the sons of Levi and refine worship until offerings are again acceptable supplies the pattern of a sudden temple-cleansing visitation. Jesus' inspecting (11:11) then purging the temple coheres with this messenger-of-the-covenant judgment, though Mark cites no words.

Hosea's 'I will drive them out of my house' for their wickedness offers a verbal parallel to Jesus driving out the temple traffickers. The link is faint and the phrase generic, but it adds to the prophetic-expulsion field around the act.

Nehemiah's reforming expulsion of profane goods from the temple chambers furnishes a historical precedent for a zealous leader cleansing the sanctuary of misuse. The coherence is typological rather than verbal, so the echo is faint and contested.

Jeremiah 7, which Jesus quotes, indicts oppression of the alien, fatherless, and widow alongside temple abuse, a complex echoed in prophetic calls for justice over cult. This widens the den-of-robbers charge into Mark's social critique, though the specific text is faint here.

The fig tree 'withered away from the roots' closely matches Hosea's judgment, 'Ephraim is smitten, their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit,' completing the barren-Israel sign begun in 11:14. The root-withering verbal contact strengthens the figural reading of the temple's coming judgment with strong coherence.

'Whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea' is most pointed if 'this mountain' is the Temple Mount/Mount of Olives, which Zechariah 14 says the LORD will split and move on the day of his coming. The eschatological mountain-moving coheres with Zechariah's geography (the entry's Mount of Olives), giving the saying a temple-judgment edge.

The psalmist's confidence though 'the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the image of mountains hurled into the sea as a figure of God's overturning power amid which the faithful do not fear. Jesus' mountain-into-the-sea saying coheres with this faith-not-fear motif, though the contact is thematic and faint.

Isaiah's 'the mountains shall depart and the hills be removed, but my kindness shall not depart' offers another prophetic image of removable mountains contrasted with steadfast faith in God. The link to Jesus' 'have faith in God' plus mountain-removal is faint and one of several candidate backgrounds, hence contested.

Jesus' demand to forgive while praying so the Father may forgive (11:25) closely tracks Ben Sira's 'Forgive thy neighbour the hurt that he hath done unto thee, so shall thy sins also be forgiven when thou prayest.' The deuterocanonical maxim's near-identical conditional reciprocity gives this strong availability and coherence as a Second-Temple background.

The authorities' challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' recalls the recurring biblical pattern of questioning a deliverer's mandate, as in 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?' against Moses. The coherence is typological (the rejected commissioned agent), so the echo is faint and contested.

Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, disputing who authorized their elevation over the assembly, is another scriptural instance of leaders contesting a divinely given authority. It supplies a faint typological backdrop to the priests' question, with low volume and no verbal anchor.

Jesus' counter-question about whether John's baptism was 'from heaven' rests on the people regarding John as a true prophet, evoking Malachi's promised Elijah who turns hearts before the day of the LORD, the figure Mark identifies with John. The Elijah-prophet background gives the baptism's heavenly origin coherence, though it is implicit here.
